The table shown summarizes both models, where $x$ is the age of the car in years.

stimulus.description: Two regression models for the selling price of a used car

items.stem: What does Model A predict for the selling price of a car whose age is $7$ years? (Round to two decimal places.)

options.text: $12.46$ thousand dollars
options.why: Leaves the intercept out of the prediction.

options.text: $45.26$ thousand dollars
options.why: Model A predicts $32.8 + 1.78(7) = 45.26$.

options.text: $42.27$ thousand dollars
options.why: Uses the equation of Model B instead of the equation of Model A.

options.text: $34.58$ thousand dollars
options.why: Substitutes $x = 1$ instead of the given value of $x$.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Calculate a predicted value from one of two given regression equations

Substitute the given value of x into the equation, using both the intercept and the slope term

key_conditions.evidence: the stem and the displayed data give every value that this check uses

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the two models is supported by the values of R-squared and $S$ in the table?

options.text: The two models explain the same percent of the variation in selling price, because both use the same variables.
options.why: Using the same variables does not give the same R-squared; the table shows different values.

options.text: Model A explains a larger percent of the variation in selling price, but its predictions are typically farther from the actual values than those of Model B.
options.why: A larger R-squared goes with a smaller $S$ here; the table shows Model A with the smaller $S$, so its predictions are typically closer.

options.text: Model A explains a larger percent of the variation in selling price ($92\%$ compared with $88\%$), and its predictions are typically closer to the actual values ($S = 1.9$ compared with $2.7$).
options.why: A larger R-squared means more of the variation is explained by the linear model, and a smaller S means that the actual values typically differ less from the predictions.

options.text: Model B explains a larger percent of the variation in selling price than Model A, and its predictions are typically closer to the actual values.
options.why: Reverses the comparison: Model A has the larger R-squared and the smaller $S$ in the table.

items.stem: Which model is more appropriate for describing the relationship, and why?

options.text: Model A, because it has the larger R-squared and the smaller $S$, so its predictions are typically closer to the actual values.
options.why: Judges the models by R-squared and $S$ alone; a curved pattern in a residual plot shows that the linear model is not appropriate.

options.text: Neither model, because the residual plots show that the data cannot be modeled with a line.
options.why: Model B's residual plot has no pattern, which supports a linear model; only Model A's residual plot shows a problem.

options.text: Both models are equally appropriate, because both use a straight line.
options.why: A straight-line model can be inappropriate; the residual plot shows whether the line describes the relationship.

options.text: Model B, because the residual plot for Model A has a curved pattern while the residual plot for Model B has no pattern.
options.why: An appropriate linear model leaves residuals with no pattern; a curved pattern in the residuals shows that a linear model is not appropriate even when R-squared is large.
